Course Description

Business is increasingly cross-border, and so are its legal problems: a single company 
answers to several legal systems at once, and its hardest decisions are rarely settled by 
looking up one rule. This course equips Year-2 students to reason about law in that 
reality. It runs as a continuous board-of-directors simulation — each group governs 
one fictional cross-border company for the whole term, meeting one shared legal 
problem each week through that company’s eyes — and moves from the foundations 
of law and the two great legal traditions, through the substantive and operational law 
businesses meet most often (product liability, IP, contracts, data, labour, competition), 
to a capstone synthesis on business crime, compliance, and entity choice. Its primary 
objective is critical thinking; its secondary objective is storytelling. AI is integrated 
every week in a declared, changing role — always paired with the student’s own 
written judgement — and is prohibited at the final capstone.

Learning Outcomes

Knowledge and Understanding (subject specific) – The student is expected to:

•  identify the sources of law and distinguish the civil-law and common-law 
traditions, including their practical consequences for business; 
•  explain the core substantive frameworks a cross-border firm meets: product 
liability, intellectual property (foundations and frontiers), contracts and the CISG, 
data and privacy, labour, and competition; 
•  describe corporate criminal liability (the ‘failure to prevent’ model), compliance, 
and how entity choice and group structure allocate risk; 
•  recognise why the same conduct is treated differently across jurisdictions, and how 
far a state’s law can reach beyond its borders. 
Cognitive / Intellectual Skills (generic) – The student is expected to:

•  analyse a genuinely contested legal-business problem from multiple perspectives 
and reach a defensible position; 
•  evaluate competing arguments honestly, including constructing the strongest case 
for a view they reject; 
•  synthesise several legal frameworks at once on a single realistic scenario; 
•  exercise critical judgement over AI output — interrogate, verify, and disagree with 
reasons. 
Key Transferable Skills (generic) – The student is expected to:

•  communicate persuasively, orally and in writing, and carry an audience to a 
decision (storytelling); 
•  collaborate effectively within a sustained team — the term-long board of directors;

segments.zh:
业务越来越跨国，其法律问题也越来越多：一家公司同时应对多个法律体系，其最困难的决策很少能通过查找一条规则来解决。本课程使二年级学生能够在现实中推理法律。

它作为一个连续的董事会模拟运行——每个小组在整个任期内管理一个虚构的跨境公司，每周通过该公司的眼睛解决一个共同的法律问题——并从法律的基础和两大法律传统，通过企业最常遇到的实体法和操作法（产品责任、知识产权、合同、数据、劳动力、竞争），到商业犯罪、合规性和实体选择的综合综合。

其主要目标是批判性思维；它的次要目标是讲故事。人工智能每周都会被整合到一个已宣布的、不断变化的角色中——总是与学生自己的书面判断相结合——并且在最后的顶点被禁止。
segments.explain: 这里的 product liability（产品责任）指：有缺陷的产品造成损害时，生产者等可能承担的责任。

• 解释跨境公司需要满足的核心实质性框架：产品责任、知识产权（基础和前沿）、合同和《销售公约》、数据和隐私、劳工和竞争；

• 描述公司刑事责任（“未能预防”模型）、合规性以及实体选择和集团结构如何分配风险；

• 认识为什么相同的行为在不同的司法管辖区会受到不同的对待，以及一个州的法律可以在多大程度上超越其边界。认知/智力技能（通用）——学生应：

segments.zh:
• 从多个角度分析真正有争议的法律商业问题，并得出可辩护的立场；

• 诚实地评估相互竞争的论点，包括为他们拒绝的观点构建最有力的论据；

• 在一个现实场景中同时综合多个法律框架；

• 对人工智能输出进行批判性判断——询问、验证和不同意理由。关键可转移技能（通用）——学生应：

COURSE CONTENT

Sessions: 
Date: 
Contents:

Session 1

Is It Legal — or Is It Right?  (Sources of Law, Legal Systems & Morality · anchor: 
Martin Luther King) 
Topics: where law comes from (sources); why legal systems disagree; the 
moral/legal distinction. 
Assessment / activity: Ungraded diagnostic case (Northwind Industries) through 
six perspectives · course orientation: boards formed, the ten companies assigned, 
the AI model and the weekly ‘Ask AI, then disagree’ paragraph introduced. No 
quiz. 
Objective: Leave able to separate ‘is it lawful?’ from ‘is it right?’ — and ready for 
the term’s working rhythm.

Session 2

Civil Law & Common Law  (anchor: Portalis) 
Topics: the two great legal traditions; codes vs precedent; good faith in 
negotiation; what the difference means for a business. 
Assessment / activity: Quiz 1 (on Session 1 pre-class) · graded group case begins: 
Pomme S.A.S. — the collapsed cross-border deal · AI role: research assistant. 
Objective: Reason inside both traditions and predict how each would treat the 
same broken negotiation.

Session 3

Product Liability  (anchor: Justice Traynor) 
Topics: negligence vs strict liability; the three defect types; how far liability 
reaches across borders. 
Assessment / activity: Quiz 2 · graded group case: Élan Mobility (defective 
product across systems) · CONTINUOUS-ASSESSMENT WEEK (heavier weighting) · 
AI role: opponent. 
Objective: Choose and defend the right liability theory for a defective-product 
scenario.

Session 4

Intellectual Property I — Foundations & Territoriality  (anchor: Victor Hugo) 
Topics: what IP protects (patent, trademark, copyright, design); why rights are 
national; cross-border infringement. 
Assessment / activity: Quiz 3 · graded group case: Solène Studio (a design copied 
abroad) · AI role: historian. 
Objective: Explain why an IP right stops at the border — and what a cross-border 
firm must do about it.

Session 5

Intellectual Property II — Frontiers: AI & Geographical Indications  (anchor: 
Stephen Thaler) 
Topics: AI inventorship and machine-made works; geographical indications; 
where current doctrine runs out.

ECOLOGICAL TRANSITION

The ecological transition enters this course through the law that increasingly enforces it — and through the 
ethical reasoning the transition demands of managers. The course’s opening distinction, that what is lawful and 
what is right are different questions, is introduced in Session 1 through a diagnostic case in which a company 
profits from a practice that is legal where it operates but banned elsewhere as harmful; students argue the 
decision from six perspectives, including those of the affected stakeholders and of the long-term institution, 
which is precisely the reasoning the ecological transition requires of business leaders.

Substantively, environmental stakes recur across the term’s weekly board work. The product-liability week 
(Session 3) examines responsibility for products that harm users and their environment, and the regulatory 
rationale for strict liability. Several of the ten fictional companies that students govern all term place ecological 
questions at the centre of their deliberations — among them a Japanese energy company, a Brazilian logistics 
firm, and a Gulf agri-technology business — so environmental exposure, sustainability-driven regulation, and 
green reputational stakes surface naturally in the cases rather than as a bolted-on module.

The term then closes on the question beneath the transition itself. The Session 10 capstone stages the 
shareholder-primacy versus stakeholder debate (Friedman against the insider-conscience pole) on a company in 
crisis, and every board must take and defend a position on what a firm owes beyond the legal minimum — to 
the people and environments it affects. Students therefore leave the course equipped to reason about 
ecological responsibility exactly where it is hardest: where the law permits conduct that judgement says should 
stop.

segments.en: ECOLOGICAL TRANSITION
segments.zh: 生态转型

segments.en: The ecological transition enters this course through the law that increasingly enforces it — and through the ethical reasoning the transition demands of managers. The course’s opening distinction, that what is lawful and what is right are different questions, is introduced in Session 1 through a diagnostic case in which a company profits from a practice that is legal where it operates but banned elsewhere as harmful; students argue the decision from six perspectives, including those of the affected stakeholders and of the long-term institution, which is precisely the reasoning the ecological transition requires of business leaders.
segments.zh:
生态转型通过日益强化的法律进入这一过程——并通过管理者的转型要求的伦理推理。该课程的开场白是，什么是合法的，什么是正确的，是不同的问题，这一点在第一节中通过一个诊断案例进行了介绍，在该案例中，一家公司从其经营所在地区合法但在其他地方因有害而被禁止的做法中获利；

学生们从受影响的利益相关者和长期机构的六个角度对这一决定进行论证，这正是生态转型所需要的商业领袖的推理。

segments.en: Substantively, environmental stakes recur across the term’s weekly board work. The product-liability week (Session 3) examines responsibility for products that harm users and their environment, and the regulatory rationale for strict liability. Several of the ten fictional companies that students govern all term place ecological questions at the centre of their deliberations — among them a Japanese energy company, a Brazilian logistics firm, and a Gulf agri-technology business — so environmental exposure, sustainability-driven regulation, and green reputational stakes surface naturally in the cases rather than as a bolted-on module.
segments.zh:
从本质上讲，环境风险在该学期的每周董事会工作中反复出现。产品责任周（第三节）审查损害用户及其环境的产品的责任，以及严格责任的监管理由。

学生们整个学期管理的十家虚构公司中，有几家将生态问题置于其审议的中心——其中包括一家日本能源公司、一家巴西物流公司和一家海湾农业技术公司——因此环境暴露、可持续发展驱动的监管和绿色声誉利害关系自然地浮现在案例中，而不是作为一个附加模块。
segments.explain: 这里的 strict liability（严格责任）指：法律在特定情形下不要求证明行为人有过错，但仍要证明其他构成条件。

segments.en: The term then closes on the question beneath the transition itself. The Session 10 capstone stages the shareholder-primacy versus stakeholder debate (Friedman against the insider-conscience pole) on a company in crisis, and every board must take and defend a position on what a firm owes beyond the legal minimum — to the people and environments it affects. Students therefore leave the course equipped to reason about ecological responsibility exactly where it is hardest: where the law permits conduct that judgement says should stop.
segments.zh:
该术语随后以过渡本身背后的问题结束。第十场会议的高潮就陷入危机的公司展开了股东至上与利益相关者的辩论（弗里德曼反对内部良心极点），每个董事会都必须就公司超出法定最低限度的义务（对受其影响的人和环境）采取并捍卫自己的立场。

因此，学生们在课程中准备好在最困难的地方推理生态责任：法律允许判决认为应该停止的行为的地方。
segments.explain: 这里的 stakeholder（利益相关者）指：会受到公司决定影响，或能影响公司决定的人与群体。
